extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy and public policy (corn trade and bounty laws)
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of normative criteria and practical arguments about bounties, drawbacks, premiums, and the regulation of the corn trade (pricing, engrossing, forestalling, and the roles of farmers, merchants, and middlemen). Useful for assessing or designing policy toward agricultural markets and trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification for bounties
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounty may be justifiable only if a particular manufacture is necessary for the defence of society and cannot otherwise be supported at home; otherwise it is unreasonable to tax the industry of the whole people to support a particular class of manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: bounties upon the exportation of British-made sail-cloth and British-made gunpowder 'may, perhaps, both be vindicated upon this principle.' Bounties given merely as favoritism in times of prosperity are idle expenses and especially absurd in times of general difficulty or distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between drawbacks and bounties (customs language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowances on exported goods that are given when the goods are exported in the same form as imported are 'drawbacks'; when the form has been altered by manufacture and the goods fall under a new denomination, the allowance is a 'bounty'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: bounty on refined sugar considered a drawback of duties on brown/Muscovado sugars; bounty on wrought silk a drawback of duties on raw/thrown silk; bounty on gunpowder a drawback of duties on brimstone and saltpetre. One must attend to the nature of the thing rather than the word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premiums to artists/manufacturers are acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Premiums (public rewards) to those who excel in particular occupations are not subject to the same objections as bounties: they encourage dexterity and ingenuity and are not large enough to distort the allocation of capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premiums tend to 'render the work... as perfect and complete as possible.' Their expense is 'very trifling' compared to bounties, which can be very large (example: bounty upon corn costing over £300,000 in one year).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid profuse bounties in hard times
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving bounties as a kind of extravagant expenditure may seem natural in great prosperity, but continuing such profusion during times of general difficulty or distress is highly absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: sustaining generous bounties when public finances are under strain; the passage contrasts private and public folly during wealth and the need for restraint in hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of the corn trade
rubrics_metrics.description: The corn trade is composed of four distinct branches: (1) inland dealer; (2) merchant-importer for home consumption; (3) merchant-exporter of home produce for foreign consumption; (4) merchant-carrier or importer to export again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy is the basis for later normative claims about which branch most affects the home market and policy priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest alignment of inland dealer and the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest of the inland corn dealer and that of the great body of the people are essentially the same: he will raise price only to what real scarcity requires and has an incentive to proportion consumption to supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: by discouraging consumption when scarce, and by risking loss if he misprices, the inland dealer is led (even unintentionally) to manage supply prudently; this alignment limits the danger of profiteering by inland dealers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of monopolising the corn supply
rubrics_metrics.description: In a civilized and extensive corn country, the nature of production (many dispersed owners, large annual consumption) makes it nearly impossible for a few large capitals to engross or monopolise corn to the detriment of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: value and production structure exceed what a few private capitals can purchase and coordinate; historical dearths/famines usually arise from scarcity of season, not combinations among inland dealers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price controls by government during dearth are counterproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: When government orders dealers to sell at a supposed 'reasonable price,' it may either discourage bringing corn to market (worsening shortage) or encourage consumption so fast as to cause famine before season's end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy anti-pattern: fixing prices in dearths; the text argues that such controls can produce famine even at the season's start or accelerate consumption that leads to famine later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unrestricted freedom of the inland corn trade as best preventive/palliative
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlimited, unrestrained freedom of the corn trade is the only effective preventive of famine and the best palliative of the inconveniences of a dearth; it deserves the full protection of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: free trade distributes scarcity over time and geography; the inland trade is far more important to the home market than import/export for supplying domestic needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engrossing/forestalling fears are largely groundless
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular fears that merchants will buy up (engross) or forestall markets to hurt the people are misplaced and comparable to fears of witchcraft; merchants buying for resale often signal genuine scarcity and serve the public by preventing worse outcomes later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a merchant misjudges and price doesn't rise, he loses; if he judges right, he prevents later severe shortages. Statutory punishments for engrossing/forestalling therefore punish potentially useful commercial behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws that forbid middlemen or force farmers to retail are unjust and impolitic
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes that prohibit manufacturers from retailing or that oblige farmers to retail (thus forcing them to divide their capital between cultivation and merchandising) are violations of natural liberty and are both unjust and harmful to economic improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: such laws obstruct division of labour, reduce cultivation, and prevent capital from being returned promptly to productive use; the farmer obliged to retail cannot cultivate as effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization/division of labour increases efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A dealer or workman who can concentrate all his stock or labour in a single branch acquires dexterity or methods that allow greater output and lower cost than if attention were divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: manufacturers selling retail would have to divide capital and would not undersell vigilant shopkeepers; similarly, farmers forced to retail lose the ability to employ capital fully in cultivation. 'Jack-of-all-trades will never be rich.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholesale dealers/corn merchants support small producers and promote cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Wholesale dealers enable producers (manufacturers or farmers) to keep capital constantly employed in production and provide a wealthy customer able to support them in adverse times; thus the wholesale/corn-merchant trade promotes production and tillage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: wholesale merchants can buy quickly, advance price, replace capital of many small producers, and help them through losses—beneficial for overall improvement of industry and land cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory price thresholds for lawful engrossing are arbitrary
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes that make engrossing lawful only above certain price thresholds (e.g., 48s. per quarter) rest on absurd popular prejudices: there is no fixed price at which engrossing or forestalling becomes dangerous to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: high prices can immediately follow harvest (not indicating engrossing), and the existence of a threshold misunderstands the incentives and effects of merchants buying up supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of importation on money price and real value
rubrics_metrics.description: Importation of foreign corn for home consumption tends to lower the money price of corn but not its real value; lowering the money price of corn can raise the real value of silver and thereby expand other industries and the home market for corn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: freer importation may slightly reduce farmers' money receipts but increases real wealth and employment; import duties tied to home-market prices (historical statutes) have been used to regulate this.
